records.table: Fundador is the Brandy de Jerez that the Domecq house first sold under that name in 1874, aged in American oak casks that once held sherry. The Solera Reserva is the young one, oak, vanilla and dried fruit, for pouring over ice or long with ginger ale.
records.story: The Domecq house of Jerez de la Frontera made its name with sherry, and by the account the brand gives it was in 1874 that it first sold a brandy under the name Fundador, the founder. The house calls it the first Brandy de Jerez. It was aged as sherry is aged: by criaderas and solera, rows of casks through which younger spirit is moved by stages towards the solera itself, so that every bottling is drawn from a blend of many ages. The three grades of Brandy de Jerez, Solera, Solera Reserva and Solera Gran Reserva, are each set by an average age drawn from such a system. The Domecq business changed hands more than once over the next century, and in 2016 the Philippine brandy maker Emperador completed its purchase of Bodegas Fundador, the Jerez cellars that make the brandy, from Beam Suntory. Behind a bar Fundador is where Spanish brandy begins: young, sherried and easy, and the bottle to reach for when a guest asks plainly for a Spanish brandy.

records.story: Sánchez Romate dates itself to 1781, when a Spanish merchant founded the business in Jerez de la Frontera, and it grew as a sherry house. In 1887, by the house's own account, the fourth generation of the family made a brandy for themselves and a close circle of friends, aged through a solera of sherry casks. They named it for Cardinal Pedro González de Mendoza (died 1495), archbishop of Toledo from 1482, who presided over the royal council of Isabella and Ferdinand and was called in his day the third king. What began as a family bottle became, as the house puts it, its flagship: the Cardenal Mendoza Solera Gran Reserva, labelled Clásico beside the older Carta Real. It is made from holandas alone and aged by criaderas and solera in American oak casks seasoned with oloroso and Pedro Ximénez, and the house gives it an average of fifteen years, five times the three the rules ask of the grade. For a bartender it is the old style of Brandy de Jerez in one bottle: dark, raisined and long, the Spanish brandy to offer after dinner.

records.story: González Byass dates itself to 1835, when a young merchant founded a sherry house in Jerez de la Frontera; an English partner, whose name the house carries, joined soon after. Its fino, Tío Pepe, named for the founder's uncle, carried the house abroad. In 1951, by the house's own account, González Byass launched Lepanto as its senior brandy. Lepanto is distilled at the house's Los Arcos bodega in Jerez, twice, in two Charentais copper pot stills of the kind used in Cognac, and from Palomino wine alone, the grape of sherry; the house describes it as made wholly in Jerez, from the still to the bottle. It then ages by criaderas and solera in American oak casks that first held Tío Pepe and then oloroso, for an average of twelve years. The range grew around it: an OV, finished in casks of old oloroso, and a PX, finished in casks of Pedro Ximénez, both given fifteen years. For a bartender Lepanto is the lesson that Brandy de Jerez can be distilled where it ages, from the grape of sherry itself.

records.story: Osborne dates itself to 1772, when, by its own account, a young English merchant founded the business at El Puerto de Santa María, the sherry town across the bay from Cádiz. Carlos I is older than its tie to Osborne. The brand dates its solera to 1889, and a brand story, told as a story, has a cellar master find forgotten casks in a corner of his bodega and name the brandy they held Carlos I. In 2008 Osborne bought the Carlos I label from Pernod Ricard España, with Carlos I Imperial, Carlos III and Felipe II, as the Spanish competition authority's file of that year records. The solera is worked in American oak casks that once held sherry, sixteen scales deep by Osborne's own report, so that the brandy drawn has an average age of about twelve years. Older bottlings followed, the Imperial XO and the 1520, a blend of three old soleras. For a bartender Carlos I is the lesson in what Solera Gran Reserva means: holandas alone, and years of sherried oak counted as an average.

records.story: Williams & Humbert was founded in Jerez de la Frontera in 1877 by two British partners, whose names it carries, and it made its name with sherry, Dry Sack among it. Its brandy came in 1945. The house's agent in Madrid, as the brand tells it, was a friend of the Duke of Alba of the day, and asked leave to name the new brandy for the family. The name honours not that duke but the third Duke of Alba, the Great Duke, a general of the sixteenth century, and the bottle carries his title as Gran Duque d'Alba. The brandy is made from young wines of Palomino and Airén grapes, distilled in pot stills, then aged by criaderas and solera in American oak casks that once held oloroso, for an average of twelve years by the house's account. An older XO followed in the range. The house's own pages often spell the name Gran Duque de Alba, while the bottle reads d'Alba. For a bartender it is the dark, raisined Gran Reserva to set beside Cardenal Mendoza when a guest wants a Spanish brandy after dinner.
